⚡ What does development look like in an age when electricity is becoming more important to the global economy, but 655 million people still live without it?
 
As the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly opens today, the world is entering what the IEA calls the “Age of Electricity.”
 
🌍 92% of the world now has access to electricity. Yet 655 million people remain without it — and 86% of them live in Sub-Saharan Africa.
 
🍳 2 billion people still rely on polluting fuels and technologies for cooking, including 970 million in Sub-Saharan Africa.
 
⚡ Meanwhile, global electricity demand is expected to grow by 3.6% annually through 2030, adding around 1,100 TWh each year.
 
💻 Data centres alone could consume around 945 TWh by 2030, more than double today’s level.
 
☀️ Renewables now provide over 30% of global electricity. But renewable generating capacity averages just 33.6 watts per person in low-income countries, compared with 1,224 watts in high-income countries — a gap of more than 36 times.
 
For me, these numbers point to a fundamental development challenge: we are building an increasingly electrified global economy, but we are not yet building it equally.
 
AI, data centres, advanced manufacturing, electric mobility and cooling are increasing the value of reliable power. Yet where energy could unlock some of the greatest development gains, hundreds of millions still lack basic access.
 
The energy transition therefore cannot be measured only in gigawatts installed or emissions avoided. We also need to ask where new capacity is built, who can access it, and what opportunities it creates.
 
As leaders gather in New York, the opportunity is to make this “Age of Electricity” an age of development too — expanding access, creating jobs and investment, and enabling more countries to participate in the industries shaping the global economy.
 
The real measure of the energy transition will not only be how much energy we produce, but how widely its opportunities are shared.
